An Oleh just reached out to share a job-search win and his strategy was simple: "Positive Chutzpah" It’s the mindset of moving fast without asking for permission. Bypass gatekeepers, drop formal pleasantries, and hand a decision-maker a direct, high-value proposition If you’re new in Israel, this level of directness might feel completely unnatural My tip: try it anyway! Be bold enough that it feels a little uncomfortable, but structure your pitch so well they have no choice but to respect the hustle There’s a fine line between annoying spam and positive chutzpah. But Israel's ecosystem is built for the latter Speed, raw execution and putting yourself out there in a vulnerable but confident way always beats polished corporate jargon and hierarchy

Multiple clients lost their jobs last week. The tech industry is brutal right now. Company after company announcing layoffs. Much of it is outside your control. Currency, AI. But there are a few things you can do: 👉 Set aside an emergency fund in shekels. Pikadon or Keren Kaspit. 3-4 months of expenses. Combined with Dmei Avtala, that should give you 6-8 months to find another job. 👉 Check that your company has been depositing your retirement savings into your pension account. Companies in financial trouble often fall behind. It's a crime to deduct pension and not transfer it. 👉 Think about what your next move would be. If starting a business is on your radar, can you start it slowly as a side hustle? 👉 Try to be indispensable. What can you do to become the most valuable employee in your department? Sending my love and support to you all. And may the dollar be with you.

Most olim sort out the basics quickly. Bank account. Kupat cholim. Driver's license. But 5 years in, there are usually 6 things still sitting undone. 1. Pension contributions aren't optimized The default track your agent put you on isn't necessarily the right one. Most people have never checked. 2. No brokerage account Many olim have money sitting in a checking account earning nothing. 3. No financial plan for buying property Most olim want to buy. Few have modeled whether they can, when, and at what cost to their other goals. 4. Insurance is patchy Are you covered if you get ill, disabled, or your spouse passes away? 5. No will or financial instructions for your spouse If something happened to you tonight, could your partner find everything and know what to do? 6. No written plan A plan with goals, timeline, tradeoffs, that you actually come back to. If any of these hit close to home, I can help.

Proof of work will beat credentials in nearly every industry. The findings of a recent study by the National Bureau of Economic Research: There have been 240% more code commits but only 30% more software releases. This was determined by analyzing data on 500K+ GitHub developers combined with their AI usage. I've spent over a decade helping teams ship features and have never seen such a discrepancy. As an early stage startup, having LLM's at your fingertips is like having the keys to a Bugatti. You can ship at warp speed. But how do you determine if customers will actually use the features the engineers spent their capacity on? Bring your highest valued users into sprint meetings WHILE you are building the features. They don't have time to attend? Fine. Maintain a consistent communication cadence with them. I learned this lesson the hard way in a prior corporate role. With the Compliance MD as our stakeholder, we had what appeared to be well-defined requirements for enhancements to a reporting dashboard at the start of the sprint. As the sprint progressed, being able to reach the MD throughout the sprint was nearly impossible due to the nature of corporate: multiple layers of management and playing the game of telephone across the layers. As you could guess, the release was an utter disaster and required us to go back to the drawing board. The same communication breakdowns are prevalent at rapidly scaling Series A & B startups. Consistent engagement and communication with the customer while building the product features means faster feedback cycles. And faster feedback cycles mean shipping features that the customer would actually use. This is just ONE of the aspects of the delivery system that I help early stage startups dial in. It's time for early stage startups to put customers first instead of shipping for clout. If this sounds all too familiar, connect with me for a free scoping call.

One of a trader's most valuable skills is knowing what would change their mind. My U.S. equities career began in 2006. Over the next two decades, my work took me through trading, developing traders, market microstructure and professional execution environments—and into systems design and LLM agent development. One lesson connects that journey: a trading decision has a life beyond the signal. It begins with how a trader interprets context, allocates attention and decides whether to act. It continues through order routing, broker and clearing dependencies, execution monitoring and the moments when someone needs to intervene. That is the perspective I bring to financial AI. What information did the trader have at the time? What would change their conviction—or make them wait? What happens when an order partially fills, a request is rejected or the system loses track of state? How should an agent recognize uncertainty and hand control back to a person? These questions connect three areas of my work: • Trader decision intelligence: translating tacit judgment, situational awareness and decision boundaries into structured context and testable scenarios. • Institutional execution workflows: understanding how trading intent becomes orders, executions and operational outcomes across professional platforms and API-enabled environments. • LLM agent development: connecting domain requirements with tools, orchestration, evaluation, monitoring and human oversight. For AI teams, this combination can make hidden assumptions explicit before they become expensive engineering decisions. It is also the foundation for CatalystDesk. I am building toward reusable decision knowledge, evaluation tools and workflow software for financial AI. Expert-led design partnerships are a route to discovering recurring needs and turning them into products that many teams can use. A company doesn’t become organized by hiring more people. Sometimes, hiring solves a capacity problem. But when the underlying workflow is inefficient, additional people can simply create more coordination. More requests need approval. More transactions need tracking. More departments need access to financial information. Eventually, the company needs better systems—not just a bigger team. This is particularly relevant as businesses introduce AI agents into their operations. An AI agent should have a defined role, an identity, and clearly established financial authority. COASTA’s backend architecture supports organizational roles, separate AI-agent identities, and configurable spending controls. These foundations are designed to help businesses introduce financial automation without treating every participant as having the same permissions. For founders, scaling should mean increasing operational capacity without losing control. Growth creates complexity. Good infrastructure helps manage it. AI did something for entrepreneurs this year that software spent a decade promising: it made them builders. People who never wrote a line of code now have a morning briefing they put together themselves in Claude, or a weekly cash view ChatGPT assembles for them every Friday. Nobody shipped it to them. They built it, fitted to their own business, and it’s often better than anything off the shelf. The one block they couldn’t plug in was their own account. From today they can. Finom MCP gives those workflows direct access to a Finom account: transactions, invoices, cards, and bookkeeping for those who keep it with us. It reads and answers. It doesn’t move money. Your own login, only what your role already sees, and you switch it off whenever you like. Alex Gromadzki asked a good question yesterday: will we all end up working out of one assistant, or keep moving between apps, each doing what it’s best at? My answer is that it’s not ours to decide. The entrepreneur decides, and a financial platform built for entrepreneurs has to be comfortable with that. So we built on the open standard, and we start with read access. If building your own tools isn’t your thing, Finom AI inside the app does the same job for you. Either way, the admin should take less of your week. Kudos to Ivo Dimitrov , Kristjan Kaar , Alex Gromadzki , Daria Rumiantseva and the whole team behind this. #Finom #FinomAI #FinomMCP

Maor, totally agree on the window. One distinction though: the models know how a bank ledger works in theory, not how your specific bank defines net exposure, an active patient, or recognized revenue. And in regulated industries, that exact definition is what the regulator actually checks. We see this all the time at Sisense. Incumbents have those definitions buried across 20 years of old dashboards and reports that nobody fully trusts anymore. The new entrant's real edge isn't just skipping legacy software. It's the chance to lock down clear, governed definitions from day one so every agent works off the same answer. Maybe the hard companies of the next decade win on trusted context, not code.

I agree that software is becoming crowded, especially in B2B. So much attention seems focused on AI infrastructure and business tools, while there’s still a gap in B2C applications built on top of the main AI agents to help people in their everyday lives

Agree, and I think the hardest part of a bank or a hospital isn't the regulation, it's trust. They'll let a startup run a pilot quickly, but getting to production takes a long stretch of security reviews and one person inside willing to put their name on you. Founders who plan for that from day one are the ones who make it.

I agree, and the money is already following. VCs are writing much bigger checks into hard companies, because that's where the large capital requirements and the real moats are. I think we'll see more SaaS founders bootstrapping, and VC money going into hard companies that need much larger investments.

The model knows the ledger. The clean ledger. Hard industries run on the messy one. The exceptions. The phone calls. The judgment calls that never made it into a document. I met today with Naftali Dratman , an entrepreneur from Beit Shemesh who helps American companies in biotech, manufacturing, and other industries find the right tech solutions by connecting them with Israeli startups. What stood out to me most was not just what he does, but how he does it. Naftali is a serious networker, but his networking is built around giving. He interviews people in the startup world, highlights their stories through his podcast and newsletter, and constantly looks for ways to connect people who can help each other. His mindset is very much “go-giver,” not just “go-getter.” It was a good reminder that the best networking is not about asking, “What can I get from this person?” It’s about asking, “How can I help?”
